newsitem.title: UK: Best is yet to come for UK gilts - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Best is yet to come for UK gilts - analysts.

text.p: UK gilts paused for breath on Monday and traded sideways after a week of heady gains, but analysts and traders said they were confident of more net gains and outperformance in the months ahead.

"The new powers granting the Bank of England independence and rumours last week, though probably scurrilous, that the UK might consider ERM membership have elevated the status of gilts within the euro area," said Philip Shaw, group economist at Union Plc.
He said gilts were now on track to achieve the same yield differential to Bunds as Swedish government bonds, around 121 basis points, within weeks.
The yield spread to Bunds edged up to 139 basis points on Monday from 134 on Friday as some traders took profit and unwound convergence trades.

A rash of convergence trades -- deals that take advantage of UK gilt yields converging with other European bond yields -- were executed after last Tuesday's surprise decision to grant the Bank of England operational independence.

Although the central bank's new powers fall short of the criteria laid down for European economic and monetary union in the Maastricht Treaty, Chancellor Gordon Brown's decision was seen as a significant step on the road to signing up.

Until the announcement, gilts yielded more than bonds from every other major European market with the exception of Italy. They were quoted to yield around 175 basis points over Bunds after the May 1 election.
Traders said convergence trades, mostly against Bunds, would help to drive the market higher and narrow the yield spread in the weeks ahead.
"Some people have taken profit but there is still a lot of interest in selling that spread, so there is plenty of confidence that gilts will outperform even more," said one trader at a GEMM.
"I can see the spread easily making 120 by the end of June."
Steven Andrew, gilts analyst at Merrill Lynch, is even more bullish on the outlook for the UK market.
"We're setting a three month target for the spread of 100 basis points, 82 in six months and 63 in 12 months."

Much of the outperformance forecast by Merrill is based on German Bund yields rising. "We think German growth will bounce quite sharply, the mark will stay weak and fiscal policy will stay loose ahead of the election there."
And the newly empowered Bank of England will underpin gilts. "We expect the Bank to retain its hawkish view on inflation. We'll get the first evidence for that on Tuesday."
On Tuesday, the Bank publishes its quarterly inflation report.

Even the short end, surprisingly resilient given the accepted wisdom that an independent central bank means higher rates, may have good days ahead. "If the government can take radical action like making the Bank independent, it can take radical action on the fiscal side," said Shaw. "We could see taxes being raised in the budget, taking the pressure off monetary policy, allowing the short end to stay firm."
The new government has not set a date yet for the mini-budget, but there is speculation it will be June 10.
Brown has already promised one tax rise, a windfall levy on privatised utilities, but there is speculation there will be additional fiscal tightening to help cool consumer demand.
Some economists say Brown may elect to abolish tax relief on mortgages as a palatable alternative to higher interest rates.
"That would have the added benefit of directly hitting the housing market where price pressures have been building for well over a year," said the trader
